title: False sharing and cache-line padding
summary: Why threads writing different variables can still slow each other down: the cache line is the unit of coherence. Learn the MESI ownership dance, model its cost, and fix it with padding, alignment and private data.
outcomes: Explain why writes to different variables on one cache line force the line to move between cores
Trace MESI states and Request For Ownership messages for two cores writing one line
Compute the slowdown of a shared line versus padded data with a simple ownership-transfer model
Choose between privatizing, thread-local data, and padding with alignment, and spot padding that fails to align
Use perf c2c to tell false sharing from true sharing and pick 64 or 128 byte padding

lessons.title: Four independent counters that refuse to scale

blocks.md:
From the cache hierarchy course you know that caches never move single bytes: they move whole **cache lines**, 64 bytes on typical x86-64 parts. From the threads course you know that threads of one process share one address space, so two threads can write to neighboring addresses.

This course is about what happens when those two facts meet.

Here is the setup. Four threads each count events in their own slot of a shared array. No thread ever reads or writes another thread's slot, so there is no data race and no lock. An **atomic add** (`fetch_add`) is a read-modify-write that no other thread can interrupt halfway; with `memory_order_relaxed` it adds no ordering rules, just the indivisible update.

blocks.caption: Each thread touches only counts[id]. The code is correct; the question is how fast it runs.

blocks.prompt: Each thread does the same amount of work on its own core. Compared with one thread doing one slot, how long should four threads take to finish?
blocks.reveal: Logic says about the same time, since the work runs in parallel. Measurements say otherwise. Ulrich Drepper ran exactly this experiment (threads that only increment their own memory location 500 million times, pinned to separate processors on a 4-socket Pentium 4 machine). When each thread's location was on its own cache line, the program scaled with no penalty. When the locations were moved onto **one** cache line, he reported an overhead of 390%, 734% and 1,147% for 2, 3 and 4 threads, computed by dividing the one-line run time by the separate-line run time.

blocks.title: Drepper's measured penalty for sharing one line

scenes.caption: Separate cache lines: the blue baseline in Drepper's figure scales with no penalty. Drepper's percentages below are the one-line time divided by this baseline time.
Same work, all counters on one line: reported overhead grows with every thread added. Nothing in the source code changed except where the counters live.

blocks.md: Why would location matter? Put the addresses through the cache. Suppose `counts` starts at address `0x1000`. Each counter is 8 bytes, so they sit at `0x1000`, `0x1008`, `0x1010` and `0x1018`. The line number is the address divided by 64: all four give line `0x40`. To the cache, the four counters are one object.

scenes.caption: Each row is one 64-byte line split into eight 8-byte slots. All four counters (c0 to c3) land in line 0x40, at offsets 0, 8, 16 and 24.
Thread 0 writes c0. To write, its core must hold the entire line 0x40, so it takes all 64 bytes, including c1, c2 and c3.
Thread 1 now writes c1. Its core must take line 0x40 away from core 0. The line moves even though c0 and c1 are unrelated.
Threads 2 and 3 join, and the single line keeps moving between four cores. Every move stalls the core that wants it.
Fix preview: space the counters 64 bytes apart. Now c0 to c3 sit in lines 0x40 to 0x43, and each core keeps its own line.

blocks.md:
This is **false sharing**: threads access *different* variables that happen to share a cache line, and at least one of them writes. The hardware cannot tell the variables apart, so it behaves as if the threads shared data.

Compare **true sharing**, where threads really access the same variable (a shared counter or a lock). True sharing needs coordination by design. False sharing is pure accident of layout.
The unit of sharing between cores is the cache line, not the variable. Two variables in one line are shared as far as the hardware is concerned, whatever the source code says.

Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

blocks.question: With 64-byte lines, which pair of 8-byte variables can falsely share a line?
options: A at 0x2000 and B at 0x2040
A at 0x2038 and B at 0x2040
A at 0x2010 and B at 0x2030
A at 0x2000 and B at 0x2080
blocks.explain: Divide by 64: 0x2010 and 0x2030 are both in line 0x80 (offsets 16 and 48). 0x2038 is in line 0x80 but 0x2040 starts line 0x81, so adjacent addresses can still be on different lines. Distance alone does not decide it; the line boundary does.

blocks.question: Two threads write different fields of one struct that fits in a single cache line. A colleague says this cannot be slow because nothing is shared. What is the best reply?
options: Right, the compiler places each field on its own line automatically
Right, only atomic variables can cause cache contention
Wrong, but only because the struct needs a mutex
Wrong, the fields share one cache line, so each write forces the line to move between cores
blocks.explain: Compilers pack fields together to save space; they do not spread them across lines. Any write needs the whole line, so the two cores fight over it. No mutex is needed for correctness here, because the fields are distinct; the problem is purely performance.

lessons.title: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership

blocks.md: Each core has a private L1 data cache, so the same line can be cached in several places at once. A **cache coherence protocol** keeps those copies consistent. Drepper sums up its rules in two lines: a dirty (modified) line is present in only one cache, and clean copies can live in any number of caches.

The classic protocol is **MESI**, named for the four states a line can be in, per cache:

- **Modified (M)**: this core changed the line, and it is the only copy in any cache.
- **Exclusive (E)**: unchanged, and known not to be in any other cache.
- **Shared (S)**: unchanged, and maybe also in other caches.
- **Invalid (I)**: the slot holds nothing usable.

blocks.title: MESI states of one line in one core's cache

scenes.caption: Every line starts Invalid. The interesting question is what a core must do before it may write.
A core reads a line nobody else holds: it becomes Exclusive. A later write needs no announcement, because no other copy exists.
If other cores also hold the line, a read leaves it Shared. Many readers can sit in Shared at once at no extra cost.
Writing a Shared line requires a Request For Ownership (RFO): all other copies are invalidated before this core goes to Modified.
The flip side: when another core issues an RFO for a line this core holds Modified, this core hands over the data and drops to Invalid. Its next access misses.

blocks.md: The expensive step is the **Request For Ownership (RFO)**. Drepper describes it plainly: if a second processor wants to write a line that the first holds Modified, the first sends the line's contents and marks its own copy Invalid. Drepper calls RFO messages the point where things are going to be slow, and notes the cost is somewhat smaller, but still there, between cores on the same chip.

scenes.caption: Core 0 wants to write c0 and has no copy of line 0x40. It sends an RFO and receives the line in Modified state.
Core 1 wants to write c1, a different variable in the same line. It must also own the line, so it sends its own RFO.
Core 0 ships the whole 64 bytes over and drops to Invalid. Core 1 gets the line in Modified state and does its write.
Core 0's next increment of c0 misses. The RFO goes back the other way and the line returns to core 0. This cycle repeats for as long as both loops run.

blocks.md: Simplified: real processors implement more elaborate versions of MESI and track lines with on-chip structures rather than snooping one shared bus. The rule that matters here holds everywhere: only one core can hold a line in a writable state at a time.

blocks.prompt: Change the experiment: thread 0 keeps writing c0, while threads 1 to 3 only *read* c1, c2 and c3 in the same line. Is there still a problem?
blocks.reveal: Yes. Each write by core 0 needs ownership, which invalidates the readers' Shared copies, so their next reads miss and must fetch the line again, which in turn moves core 0's copy out of Modified. Reads alone are harmless (any number of Shared copies can coexist, which is why Drepper says constants can be grouped freely), but **one writer is enough** to make neighbors on the same line pay. OpenJDK's JEP 142 defines the problem exactly this way: two locations used by different cores on one line, with at least one core writing.

blocks.md: False sharing needs three things at once: two or more cores, one cache line, and at least one writer. Remove any one (single thread, separate lines, or read-only data) and the line stops bouncing.

blocks.question: Which access pattern causes the most coherence traffic on one 64-byte line?
options: Eight threads each read a different 8-byte field
One thread repeatedly writes all eight fields
Two threads on different cores each write their own field
Eight threads read the same field
blocks.explain: Reads leave the line Shared in every cache with no ongoing traffic. A single writer keeps the line Modified in its own cache with no one to invalidate. Two writers on different cores each need an RFO before each write after the other one wrote, so the line ping-pongs.

blocks.question: Core 0 holds line L in Exclusive state and writes to it. What must happen first?
options: Nothing: Exclusive means no other copy exists, so the line silently becomes Modified
An RFO is broadcast to invalidate other copies
The line is written back to main memory
Core 0 must first move the line to Shared
blocks.explain: That is the whole point of the Exclusive state: Drepper notes a local write in E does not have to be announced, and that E to M is much faster than S to M. Trouble starts only once another core also wants the line.

lessons.title: Putting a price on the ping-pong

blocks.md:
To reason about how bad false sharing gets, build a small cost model. It is deliberately simple; the goal is to see which knobs matter, not to predict a real chip to the cycle.

- $k$ threads, each doing $n$ writes to its own variable.
- A write to a line the core already owns costs $h$ cycles.
- Moving ownership of a line to another core costs $C$ cycles.
- While a core owns the line, it gets $b$ writes in before another core takes it away.

With padding, every core owns its own line forever, so the threads run fully in parallel and finish in $n h$ cycles. With all variables on one line, only one core can write at a time. Every write is serialized, and every $b$ writes also pay one transfer.

blocks.tex: T_{\text{padded}} = n\,h, \qquad T_{\text{shared}} = k\,n\left(h + \frac{C}{b}\right), \qquad S = \frac{T_{\text{shared}}}{T_{\text{padded}}} = k\left(1 + \frac{C}{b\,h}\right)\ \ (k \ge 2)
blocks.caption: Slowdown S of shared versus padded under the simplified model. With k = 1 there is nobody to steal the line, so S = 1.

blocks.md:
Worked example, with illustrative values $h = 1$ cycle and $C = 100$ cycles, $k = 4$ threads, $n = 10^8$ writes each:

- Padded: $T = 10^8$ cycles.
- Shared, worst case $b = 1$ (the line moves on every write): $T = 4 \times 10^8 \times 101 = 4.04 \times 10^{10}$ cycles, so $S = 404$.
- Shared, $b = 50$ (each core batches 50 writes per visit): $T = 4 \times 10^8 \times 3 = 1.2 \times 10^9$ cycles, so $S = 12$.

blocks.title: Two cores sharing one line versus owning their own

scenes.caption: Model with h = 1, C = 100, b = 4. Core 0 owns the line and does 4 writes in 4 cycles. Core 1 has asked for the line and waits.
After a 100-cycle transfer, core 1 writes 4 times while core 0, now Invalid, waits its turn.
Over 420 cycles the two cores complete 20 writes together. Most of the timeline is waiting for the line to arrive.
Padded: each core owns its line and writes every cycle. In the same 420 cycles the pair completes 840 writes, 42 times more. Over a long run the ratio approaches the model's S = 2 x (1 + 100/4) = 52.

blocks.title: Slowdown from sharing one line, by thread count

scenes.caption: With b = 50 and C = 100 the model gives S = 6, 12 and 24 at 2, 4 and 8 threads: the shared version gets slower in total as you add threads, while padded stays flat.
Worst case b = 1: every write moves the line, and S reaches 404 at 4 threads. Real cores buffer stores and usually get several writes per visit, which is why measured penalties are smaller.
Lower C models cores that share a cache level close by, so transfers are cheap. The penalty shrinks but still grows linearly with k, because writes to one line are always serialized.

blocks.md: Two consequences fall out of the model. First, the shared version is not just slower than padded, it is slower than **one thread**, because $k$ threads do $k$ times the work through a single serial point. Second, the transfer cost $C$ depends on distance. Drepper saw large penalties between separate processor sockets but only a slight, flat overhead on a single-package quad-core Core 2, even though its cores were split across two separate L2 caches. In the perf c2c guide by Joe Mario, transfers that cross NUMA nodes (remote HITMs) are called out as the most expensive kind.

Simplified model: real chips overlap work with store buffers and out-of-order execution, prefetch, and have varying transfer latency by core distance. Use the model for direction and scaling, and measure the actual number on your hardware.

blocks.question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
blocks.explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

blocks.question: A team moves the threads in a false-sharing benchmark from two sockets onto two cores of one socket and the slowdown drops a lot. What does that show?
options: False sharing is fixed
The compiler removed the shared writes
Same-socket cores do not use cache coherence
The transfer cost C fell because the cores are closer, but writes are still serialized
blocks.explain: Only C changed. The line still moves between two private L1 caches, and the k factor in S remains. Placement can hide the problem on one machine and expose it on another, which is why Drepper recommends testing on real SMP (multi-processor) machines.

lessons.title: Fixing it: pad, align, or stop sharing writes

blocks.md:
There are four standard fixes, in roughly the order you should consider them:

1. **Do not share writes at all.** Accumulate in a local variable (a register or the thread's stack) and combine results once at the end.
2. **Thread-local storage.** Drepper notes that `__thread` variables get a separate area per thread, so false sharing is not a problem unless the program creates one artificially.
3. **Pad and align** each hot per-thread item to its own line.
4. **Group by access pattern.** Keep read-only and read-mostly data away from data that is written often.

blocks.caption: The cheapest fix, when the algorithm allows it. The shared line is touched once per thread instead of n times.

blocks.md: When threads really must update shared memory as they go (statistics read live, queue indices), give each hot item its own line. C++17 added `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` for exactly this: the minimum offset between two objects to avoid false sharing. `alignas` makes the object start on a boundary of that size, and the compiler rounds the object's size up to a multiple of its alignment, which supplies the padding.

blocks.caption: C++ uses alignas on the type; crossbeam's documentation uses the head and tail of a queue as its example of fields to keep apart.

blocks.prompt: Instead of alignas, someone writes `struct Slot { long count; long sum; char pad[48]; };` (exactly 64 bytes) and puts 3 of them in an array that happens to start 56 bytes into a cache line. Is each thread's data now on its own line?
blocks.reveal: No. Padding fixes the **size** but not the **start address**. With the array at offset 56, thread 0's `count` sits in the last 8 bytes of one line and its `sum` in the first 8 bytes of the next line, which also holds thread 1's `count`. Every boundary is shared between two neighbors, so the false sharing is back. Size and alignment are both needed, which is why `alignas` and `CachePadded` set the alignment, not just the size.

scenes.caption: Aligned: three 64-byte slots start at a line boundary (0x2000). Thread t's count and sum sit together in line 0x80 + t, and no line holds two threads' data.
Same 64-byte slots starting at 0x2038, offset 56. Thread 0's count is at the end of line 0x80 and its sum at the start of line 0x81.
Line 0x81 now holds t0.sum and t1.cnt; line 0x82 holds t1.sum and t2.cnt. Each boundary line has two writers, so it ping-pongs exactly as before.

blocks.md: Padding has a price, and Drepper names it: putting every variable on its own line would blow up the program's footprint, so be selective. The numbers grow fast. 64 per-thread 8-byte counters packed together take 512 bytes, which is 8 lines. Padded to 64 bytes they take 4,096 bytes; padded to 128 bytes, 8,192 bytes. For a queue with two `CachePadded` indices and a buffer pointer, the struct grows from 24 bytes to 384 bytes on x86-64, where `CachePadded` uses 128.

scenes.caption: Packed: 64 x 8 = 512 bytes, only 8 cache lines, but every line has 8 writers.
Padding to 64 bytes gives each counter a private line: 64 x 64 = 4,096 bytes, 8 times more.
Padding to 128 bytes, the conservative choice for x86-64 discussed next lesson: 8,192 bytes, 16 times the packed size.

blocks.md: A fix needs both size and alignment: each hot item must start on a line boundary and be at least a line long. And pad only data that different threads write often; group everything else tightly.

blocks.question: Eight threads update a shared histogram with 1,000,000 buckets of 8 bytes; updates land on random buckets. What is the best fix?
options: Give each thread a private histogram and merge them at the end
Pad every bucket to 64 bytes
Align the histogram array to 64 bytes
Use a bigger cache line size constant
blocks.explain: Padding every bucket would turn 8 MB into 64 MB and wreck cache use for little gain, since random buckets rarely collide. Per-thread histograms (fix 1) remove shared writes entirely, at the cost of 8 copies and one merge. Aligning the array only moves where the boundaries fall.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: `struct Stats { std::atomic<long> hits; std::atomic<long> misses; };` with `alignas(64) Stats per_thread[8];`. Each thread writes only its own element. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the array is aligned, so elements are on separate lines
Each element is only 16 bytes, so four threads' elements share each 64-byte line
alignas cannot be used on arrays
The two atomics in one element will falsely share
blocks.explain: alignas on the array aligns only its start. Each element is 16 bytes, so elements 0 to 3 share the first line and 4 to 7 the second. Put alignas on the struct type (so sizeof becomes 64) instead. Fields inside one element are written by the same thread, so they do not cause false sharing.

lessons.title: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads

blocks.md: Every fix depends on a number: the line size. Linux exposes it per cache in sysfs as `coherency_line_size`, documented as the minimum amount of data transferred from memory to cache. Hardcoding 64 is common, but the right padding is not always the line size.

crossbeam's `CachePadded` documents its choices per architecture, and they show the variety. On x86-64 it uses 128, with the comment that starting from Intel's Sandy Bridge, the **spatial prefetcher** pulls pairs of 64-byte lines at a time, so it pessimistically assumes 128-byte lines. Folly reaches the same conclusion: its microbenchmarks showed pairs of lines seeing destructive interference under heavy atomic increments on Sandy Bridge, so its fallback value (used when the standard library does not provide the C++17 constant) is 128 on x86-64.

scenes.caption: crossbeam's per-architecture N. The docs say N is just a reasonable guess, not guaranteed to match the machine you run on.
x86-64 lines are 64 bytes, yet the padding is 128 because the prefetcher couples adjacent lines. aarch64 is 128 because some big cores have 128-byte lines.

blocks.md: C++ has a portability trap here. GCC's documentation for `-Winterference-size` explains that the value of `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` depends on the `-mtune` setting, so translation units built with different tuning can disagree on a struct's layout. It advises not using these constants in library headers where ABI stability matters, and warns about such uses by default. A fixed constant you choose yourself (often 64 or 128) avoids that.

To find false sharing on Linux, use `perf c2c` (cache to cache). It samples loads and stores with their data addresses and reports the cache lines with the most **HITM** events, which Joe Mario's guide defines as a load that hit a modified cache line in another cache. Remote HITMs cross NUMA nodes and cost the most.

blocks.code:
perf c2c record ./counter_bench         # sample loads and stores
perf c2c report --stdio                 # hottest lines, then per-offset detail
perf c2c report --stdio --double-cl     # group pairs of lines (adjacent-line prefetch)
blocks.caption: Commands from the perf-c2c man page. --double-cl treats lines as double size for CPUs with adjacent cache line prefetch.

nodes.label:
pad, align or
privatize the fields

scenes.caption: Record while the workload runs. perf samples memory accesses together with their data addresses.
The Shared Data Cache Line Table ranks cache lines by HITM count. A line near the top with many HITMs is contended.
The Pareto table lists each accessed offset inside that line, with code address, source line and CPUs. This is where you tell the two cases apart.
Many threads on one offset is true sharing: fix the algorithm. Different offsets written by different threads is false sharing: separate the fields.

blocks.md:
Real systems bake these fixes into their APIs:

- **Linux kernel**: `____cacheline_aligned_in_smp` aligns a field or struct to the cache line size in SMP builds and expands to nothing on uniprocessor builds.
- **Java**: JEP 142 (JDK 8) added padding for fields marked `@Contended`. HotSpot pads 128 bytes by default (`ContendedPaddingWidth`), and `RestrictContended` limits the annotation to trusted classes by default. `LongAdder`'s cells are `@Contended`, so threads that collide spread over padded cells.
- **Rust**: crossbeam's queues keep head and tail in separate `CachePadded` fields.

Do not pad on a hunch. Padding costs memory and can push other hot data out of cache, which is why Drepper calls padding every variable unacceptable. Confirm with perf c2c or a before-and-after benchmark that the line is really contended.

blocks.question: A queue pads head and tail to 64 bytes each, yet still scales badly on x86-64. `perf c2c report --double-cl` shows heavy HITMs on one line pair: offset 0x0 written by `push` threads and 0x40 by `pop` threads. Likely cause?
options: True sharing on one variable
A compiler bug
False sharing caused by adjacent-line prefetching, since 0x0 and 0x40 are neighboring 64-byte lines
The two functions are on the same core
blocks.explain: Offsets 0x0 and 0x40 are 64 bytes apart, so with 64-byte lines they are different lines. When they still show up together, the adjacent-line (spatial) prefetcher pairing is the suspect; perf c2c's --double-cl option groups lines in pairs for exactly this. Padding to 128, as crossbeam and folly do on x86-64, is the usual fix.

blocks.question: Why might a library avoid `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` in a public header?
options: Its value can change with compiler tuning flags, so separately built code may disagree on struct layout
It is not defined in C++17
It is always 64, which is too small
It only works with std::atomic members
blocks.explain: GCC sets it from -mtune, and its documentation warns that all translation units relying on it must use the same tuning. In a public header that is an ABI hazard, so libraries often use a fixed constant such as 128 instead.
